Normally the portal would redirect her to HTTPS straight away. Unknown to Alice, an attacker on the same coffee shop WiFi network is running an SSL strip attack: the attacker intercepts that first plain HTTP request, talks HTTPS to the real portal, and keeps Alice's side of the connection on HTTP. The page loads normally, but without encryption.

The payroll portal looks exactly as Alice remembers - the Meridian logo, the familiar blue color scheme, the standard login form. She enters her work credentials without hesitation.

steps.name: Heeding the Warning

Instead of the dashboard, Alice sees a stark warning: "Your connection is not private." She's not sure what caused it, but the warning looks serious.

The certificate warning appeared because the MITM attacker tried to intercept this HTTPS connection too, but the browser detected the invalid certificate and blocked the page. Alice decides not to proceed.

The $4,750 unauthorized withdrawal from her personal bank and the work account compromise both trace back to the coffee shop session two days ago.

steps.description:
Alice's stomach drops. The unauthorized bank withdrawal. The suspicious login from Ukraine. Both came in the days after she used the coffee shop WiFi.

She reads the IT Security alert again, this time with growing dread.
steps.instructions: Review the security alert to understand the connection.

steps.name: The Missing Padlock

highlighterTexts: The site loaded over HTTP - not HTTPS. There is no padlock icon in the address bar.
Without HTTPS, everything Alice entered - her password, routing number, account number - was transmitted completely unencrypted and visible to the attacker on the same WiFi network.
This happened because of an SSL strip attack: the attacker intercepted Alice's connection and silently removed the encryption, so the page loaded over plain HTTP instead of secure HTTPS.

steps.description: Alice navigates back to the payroll portal to examine it with fresh eyes. She notices something in the address bar she completely overlooked before.
steps.instructions: Look at the browser's security indicator.

steps.name: What Is a Man-in-the-Middle Attack?
steps.description:
What Alice experienced is called a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack. Here's how it works:
  • Open WiFi = No protection. Anyone on the same network can see and intercept traffic that isn't encrypted.
  • The attacker sits "in the middle" between Alice's computer and the internet, silently relaying and recording everything.
  • SSL stripping is a specific MITM technique where the attacker catches a plain HTTP request before the site can redirect it to HTTPS, and keeps the connection on HTTP, removing encryption without the user noticing. Sites that enforce HTTPS with HSTS are protected.
  • The domain was real - this wasn't a fake website. The attacker intercepted the connection to the legitimate payroll portal.
  • The most visible clue was the missing padlock icon and "http://" instead of "https://" in the address bar.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Warning That Protected You

highlighterTexts: The certificate warning appeared because the MITM attacker tried to intercept this connection too - but the browser caught it. The attacker couldn't forge a valid security certificate.
Unlike the payroll portal (opened from a plain http:// link, so SSL stripping could keep it on HTTP), this site enforces HTTPS with HSTS.
The browser only ever connects to it over HTTPS, so it checked the attacker's certificate, found it invalid, and blocked the page.
Key contrast: SSL stripping succeeds silently (check the padlock!), but certificate warnings are your browser actively protecting you. Never ignore them.

Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting this promptly. Our investigation confirms you were the victim of a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack while using public WiFi at the coffee shop.

What we found:
  • An attacker on the CafeConnect WiFi network performed an SSL strip attack, catching your plain http:// request to the payroll portal and keeping the connection on HTTP instead of letting it upgrade to HTTPS

email.subject: Re: Incident Report - Man-in-the-Middle Attack

highlighterTexts: The attacker used SSL stripping to silently remove encryption. Alice's credentials and bank details were transmitted in plain text, visible to anyone on the same network.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Alice's quick report helped contain the damage, but the experience taught critical lessons about HTTPS, public WiFi, and Man-in-the-Middle attacks:
  • Always check for the padlock - HTTPS encrypts your data in transit. If the padlock is missing, your data is being sent in plain text for anyone on the network to intercept. A padlock means encrypted, not genuine: phishing sites have one too
  • Never ignore certificate warnings - They can mean someone or something is interfering with the encrypted connection. Click "Back to safety" - the warning is your browser protecting you
  • Public WiFi is inherently dangerous - Open networks with no password allow anyone nearby to intercept traffic. Attackers can silently strip HTTPS encryption without you noticing
  • Always use a VPN on public networks - A VPN encrypts your traffic between your device and the company network, so an attacker on the same WiFi cannot read or tamper with it
  • Trust your password manager - If autofill doesn't offer to fill your credentials, the site may not be what you expect. A missing autofill prompt is a subtle but important clue
  • Report incidents immediately - Fast reporting helps contain financial damage, protect colleagues, and shut down active attacks
On a site you sign in to, a missing padlock means your data is exposed. A present one only means the connection is encrypted, so still check the address.

steps.name: Types of Download Attacks

The DesignSuite Pro 'security patch' Alice downloaded was this type of attack.

Behavior red flags: downloads that start automatically, website notifications claiming urgent updates.
Multiple redirects before reaching the download page and browser warnings about unsafe downloads.
Social engineering red flags: urgency ('update now or risk data loss'), authority ('from your IT department').

  • Verify the extension is on your company's approved software list
If you suspect a compromised extension:
  • Remove it immediately from your browser
  • Report the incident to IT Security without delay
  • Change passwords for any accounts accessed while the extension was active
Ongoing habits:
  • Audit your installed extensions regularly and remove anything you no longer use
  • Review permission changes when extensions update - new permissions may indicate a supply chain attack
  • Apply the principle of least privilege: only grant the minimum permissions an extension needs
